    What is the difference between a snow squall and a blizzard?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    A snow squall is a short, intense burst of snow and wind (minutes to an hour), causing sudden, dangerous whiteout conditions, while a blizzard is a longer, more widespread storm (3+ hours) defined by specific criteria: sustained winds of 35+ mph, near-zero visibility (less than 1/4 mile), and heavy snow (falling or blowing), making the key differences duration, intensity, and official criteria.
     
    Snow Squall
    • Duration: Very short, typically 30-60 minutes. 
    • Intensity: Sudden, heavy snow and strong, gusty winds, creating rapid whiteout conditions. 
    • Impact: Extremely hazardous for travel due to sudden visibility loss, akin to a summer severe thunderstorm. 
    • Official Alert: A newer term, similar to a severe thunderstorm warning. 
    Blizzard
    • Duration: Must last for at least 3 hours. 
    • Intensity: Sustained winds or frequent gusts of 35 mph or greater, reducing visibility to less than 1/4 mile from falling and/or blowing snow. 
    • Impact: Widespread, long-lasting severe conditions with significant snow accumulation. 
    • Official Alert: A specific, criteria-based warning for prolonged severe winter weather. 
    In Summary
    Think of a snow squall as a quick, intense "whiteout punch" that passes quickly, while a blizzard is a prolonged "winter siege" with official wind and visibility benchmarks. Both are dangerous, but a blizzard has stricter, longer-lasting criteria.

      How long do snow squalls usually last?
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Snow squalls are short, intense bursts of snow, typically lasting 30 to 60 minutes, though some can be even shorter or extend up to a few hours, bringing whiteout visibility and icy roads quickly before passing, unlike longer snowstorms. They're characterized by heavy snow, strong winds, and sudden visibility drops, creating dangerous travel conditions that require immediate action like slowing down and using hazard lights, say the National Weather Service (NWS) and others.
       
      Key Characteristics
      • Duration:
        Usually 30-60 minutes at one location; some may be just 15 minutes, others up to 1-3 hours. 
      • Intensity:
        Heavy snow, high winds, and near-total whiteout conditions. 
      • Impact:
        Rapidly developing slippery roads, making them extremely hazardous for drivers. 
      • Cause:
        Often associated with strong cold fronts, similar to summer thunderstorms but with snow. 
      Why They're Dangerous 
      • Suddenness:
        They can appear unexpectedly, even with clear skies nearby, creating a false sense of security.
      • Brevity:
        Their short duration means a driver might enter one mid-trip and believe it's safe because the forecast showed little snow, notes the EcoFlow blog.
      What to Do
      • Get Alerts:
        Enable Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) for "significant" snow squall warnings. 
      • If Driving:
        Slow down, turn on hazard lights, increase following distance, and get off the road if possible, waiting out the squall.

        What is the biggest risk of a snow squall?
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        The biggest risk of a snow squall is sudden, near-zero visibility and flash-frozen roads, leading to high-speed, multi-vehicle pileups and chain-reaction accidents, making travel extremely hazardous and potentially deadly, even with minimal snowfall. These conditions create a "whiteout" effect, leaving drivers with no time to react as they encounter stopped traffic, slick ice, and gusty winds all at once, causing accidents and highway shutdowns.
         
        Why Snow Squalls Are So Dangerous:
        • Sudden Whiteouts:
          Visibility can drop from clear to nothing in seconds, making it impossible to see vehicles ahead. 
        • Flash Freezes:
          Cold air rushes in, instantly turning moisture on roads into invisible black ice, creating treacherous surfaces. 
        • Rapid Deterioration:
          Conditions change so quickly that drivers have little to no time to adjust, leading to loss of control and collisions. 
        • Chain Reactions:
          The inability to see or stop creates dangerous pileups, often shutting down highways. 
        What to Do:
        • Delay Travel: Avoid being on the road if a squall is expected. 
        • Slow Down: If caught in one, reduce speed and turn on headlights. 
        • Don't Slam Brakes: This can cause skidding; maintain control. 
        • Stay Alert: Keep your phone on for Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA). 
        • Stay in Your Vehicle: If in a pileup, remain inside your car with your seatbelt on and hazard lights flashing.
